note: make rebaseline CAN BE OOM-KILLED ON THE MAC, AND NOTHING IN THE SCRIPT TELLS YOU THAT IS WHAT HAPPENED. Measured during The Escapement flip: two consecutive runs died, a DIFFERENT job each time, with no OOM message surfaced by the make output -- it reads as an ordinary non-zero exit from whichever regeneration step happened to be running. Re-running produced a different casualty, which is the tell. HV_JOBS=2 completed cleanly. THE TRAP IS NOT THE OOM, IT IS THE ATTRIBUTION. A rebaseline that dies partway leaves SOME artifacts regenerated and others not, and the natural next move -- inspect the diff, decide the partial output looks plausible, commit it -- produces a tree where a few generated files are current and the rest are stale, with every one of them tracked and none of them complaining. The drift check cannot see it because the files it compares are internally consistent; they are just not all from the same run. If a rebaseline exits non-zero, do not read its partial output as a result. Reset the generated paths, lower HV_JOBS, and run it again to completion. WHY IT BITES HERE SPECIFICALLY: a rebaseline builds release artifacts and runs two 500-seed censuses worth of derivation concurrently, which is the memory peak of the whole repo, and a campaign worktree pool means several checkouts may hold warm target directories at once. This is a 12-core Mac with other worktrees resident. On a machine with more headroom you may never see it, which is exactly why it is worth writing down rather than remembering. SECOND, SMALLER, SAME FAMILY: the same run renamed two kernel tests, which staled their rows in docs/timings/subfloor-roster.tsv. subfloor-roster.sh builds EXACT-MATCH nextest filters from that file, so a row naming a test that no longer exists selects NOTHING -- the commit gate quietly ran two fewer tests than its roster claimed and printed a green number. Repairing the rows took the gate from 483 to 485. If you rename a test, grep the roster for its old name in the same commit; nothing else will.
